stem: At intake, a consultant, 15-year-old golfer Odette, and her father agreed in writing that he would receive attendance and a brief monthly note on general progress, and that session content would stay private unless safety was at risk. After the fourth session, the father calls: Odette has been quiet after practices, and he asks what she has said about her swing coach. Nothing she has shared raises a safety concern. What should the consultant do?
options: Reassure him that nothing she has said is cause for worry, without giving any specifics
Give him a general sense of her views on the coach, since he is her legal guardian
Thank him for the concern, restate the agreement, and suggest he talk with Odette
Offer to raise his concern with her next session, then tell him how she responds
rationales: Even a reassuring summary discloses session content: saying that nothing she said is worrying is itself a report on what she said. It also teaches the father that a worried call will earn an update outside the agreement.

Parental permission was needed to begin, but the father agreed at intake, with Odette's assent, that content would stay private. Passing on her views of the coach breaks that agreement and would likely end her openness in sessions.

Once a sharing agreement is in place with the parent's permission and the minor's assent, the consultant honors it consistently: acknowledging the father's concern, reminding him what he receives (attendance and the monthly note) and what stays private absent a safety concern, and encouraging him to talk with his daughter directly. Predictable boundaries keep the arrangement trustworthy for both of them.

Carrying his concern into the session and reporting her reaction back makes the consultant a go-between, and her response is itself session content. It also pressures Odette to account for herself to her father through the consultant.
takeaway: Once parent and minor have agreed on what is shared, honor the agreement consistently, even when a worried parent asks for more.

stem: Henrik, a collegiate rower, arrives for his first session and says, "Coach told me I have to see you. Honestly, I'm not sure what we're supposed to do here." He is polite but guarded and keeps his answers short. The consultant wants to build a strong working alliance from the start. What is the most appropriate way to begin?
options: Explain what consulting involves, then ask what Henrik would want to get out of it
Ask what the coach told him, then explore those concerns together to set a focus
Outline a few common mental skills and let Henrik choose one to start practicing
Have him complete a short intake questionnaire so the session can be tailored to him
rationales: Bordin's working alliance rests on agreement about goals and tasks plus an emotional bond. For a client who doesn't know why he is there, explaining the process and the consultant's role answers his actual question, and eliciting what he wants turns a referred athlete into an active collaborator.

Starting from the coach's concerns, however collaboratively, makes the coach's agenda the frame for the work and casts the consultant as the coach's agent. The coach's view can be gathered later, with Henrik's consent, once his own goals are on the table.
Offering a choice respects autonomy, but it picks tasks before any goal is agreed and before he understands what consulting is. In the working alliance, tasks follow from shared goals.

A questionnaire can be a useful part of assessment, but assessment follows rapport and expectation-setting. Handing a guarded, coach-sent athlete a form before explaining the process is likely to deepen his wariness.
takeaway: With a referred client, explain the process and elicit the client's own goals first; the alliance starts with shared goals.

topic: Names and pronouns at team intake
stem: A consultant is starting a season-long workshop series with a collegiate track and field team of 40 athletes. The coach's roster lists each athlete's legal name. The consultant wants every athlete to be addressed by the name and pronouns they actually use, without anyone feeling pressed to disclose more than they want to. Which approach is best at the first session?
options: Check with the coach beforehand, and use the names the coach says athletes go by
Open with a go-around in which each athlete states their name and pronouns
Have each athlete list a name and pronouns on the intake form everyone completes
Give your own name and pronouns, and invite athletes to share what they go by
rationales: The coach may not know or may be wrong, and asking the coach to identify athletes who use another name can out someone without consent. It also singles some athletes out instead of offering everyone the same invitation.
A go-around normalizes sharing, but it requires every athlete to state pronouns in front of 39 teammates, which can pressure someone who is questioning or not ready to be out on this team.
Collecting names on a form is sensible, but making pronouns part of a form everyone must complete turns an invitation into a requirement. Some athletes may not want to put this in writing yet.

Modeling by sharing one's own name and pronouns, then inviting (not requiring) athletes to share the names and pronouns they use, signals respect and normalizes the practice without putting anyone on the spot. Because the roster shows legal names, the invitation covers names as well as pronouns, and the consultant then uses what athletes share consistently.
takeaway: Model sharing your own name and pronouns and invite, without requiring, clients to share theirs; then use them consistently.

stem: A professional esports organization hires a consultant to run weekly sessions with its five-player roster; the head coach and general manager will receive a monthly update on attendance and broad themes. At the first session, before any group norms have been discussed, the players exchange glances when asked how they handle tilt, and one asks, "Does this stuff get back to management?" What should the consultant do next?
options: Explain that updates cover only attendance and themes, then return to the tilt question
Describe what the updates contain, then agree on group norms, including the right to pass
Ask the players what they would want management to know, and shape the updates around it
Offer individual sessions for anything the players would rather not raise with teammates
rationales: Answering the question accurately is a good start, but returning straight to tilt skips the group agreements that make interpersonal risk-taking feel safe. Players who just signaled discomfort still have no say in how the group will handle what they share.

Psychological safety, a shared belief that the group is safe for interpersonal risk-taking, is built at the outset by being transparent about what leaves the room and co-creating norms, including the option not to share personal material. With no norms yet in place, both steps come before the tilt discussion.

Inviting input sounds empowering, but the reporting terms were already agreed with the organization and can't be redesigned by the players on the spot. Promising to reshape them sets up an expectation the consultant may not be able to keep.

Individual sessions may be valuable, but offering them sidesteps the question about management and implies that team sessions aren't safe for honest discussion. The group still needs clarity and norms of its own.
takeaway: Psychological safety in team work starts with transparent limits of confidentiality and co-created group norms, including the right to pass.

stem: Marguerite, a 52-year-old age-group triathlete, books a session nine days before her first full-distance race. She says she has "zero mental game," has never practiced any mental skills, and wants the consultant to "fix her head" in this one meeting. How should the consultant respond to her request?
options: Teach a complete pre-race routine today, and ask her to rehearse it daily until the race
Assess her skills with a brief questionnaire so the session targets her weakest area
Explain that mental skills build with practice, and agree on one or two aims for this race
Suggest she treat this race as a learning experience and begin skills training after it
rationales: Daily rehearsal is the right idea, but a complete routine built from scratch in one meeting is a lot to absorb nine days out, and it goes along with the expectation that a single session can fix things. Her expectations need to be addressed first.

A brief assessment can inform a plan, but it doesn't respond to the unrealistic expectation she has stated, and targeting her weakest area nine days out invites more change than she can consolidate before the race.

Establishing the relationship includes honest expectations about the process: mental skills are learned and need practice. With limited time, consultant and client agree on a small number of usable aims (for example, a simple race plan built on process cues) and frame longer-term work as an option afterward.

Framing the race as a learning experience may suit some athletes, but deferring all work leaves a client with a legitimate, workable request unsupported. Short, focused work is within scope when expectations are realistic.
takeaway: Set honest expectations about how mental skills develop, then agree on goals that fit the time available.

stem: A fire chief introduces a consultant to an engine company by saying, "They're here to figure out which of you is cracking under the pressure." Several firefighters fold their arms. The consultant's agreement with the department is to provide voluntary performance and stress-management support, with only aggregate attendance reported to the chief, and few crew members are expected to book individual sessions at first. What should the consultant do?
options: Correct the framing now by describing the actual role, voluntary contact, and reporting
Ask the chief to restate the program's purpose, since the description came from him
Invite the crew to voice their concerns first, then explain the role in response to them
Begin the planned session and clarify the role with each firefighter at individual check-ins
rationales: The crew has just been told the consultant is an evaluator, which makes honest participation feel risky. Clarifying the role, the voluntary nature of individual contact, and exactly what goes back to the chief, right away and respectfully, is the foundation of trust with organizational clients; a private word with the chief afterward can supplement this but not replace it.

Handing the correction back to the chief risks a second inaccurate description and signals that the consultant's role is whatever the chief says it is. Explaining the role and its limits is the consultant's own responsibility.

Inviting concerns is usually respectful, but the crew is reacting to inaccurate information. Asking firefighters to speak up while they believe they are being screened puts them at risk; they need accurate facts first.
Few firefighters will come to individual check-ins while they believe the consultant is screening them, so the correction may never reach most of the crew. Role clarity is needed in the room, now.
takeaway: When a stakeholder misstates your role, correct it with the clients promptly and respectfully; role clarity precedes trust.

stem: The head coach of a professional women's soccer club hires a consultant to work with the squad. In the planning meeting, the coach says, "After you meet with each player, tell me who's mentally tough enough to start in big games." The players have not yet been told anything about the consultant's role. What should the consultant do first?
options: Agree to share overall impressions of squad readiness, and keep individual comments private
Settle with the coach what will and won't be shared, then tell the players before any sessions
Ask the players at the first team meeting what they would be comfortable having shared
Offer a validated mental toughness assessment the coach can use in selection decisions
rationales: A squad-level summary sounds like a reasonable compromise, but it leaves the coach's request for selection input unresolved and the players uninformed about what leaves the room. Limits of confidentiality are negotiated with the coach and communicated to players before services begin.

In third-party arrangements the consultant clarifies at the outset who the client is, what role the consultant will play (for example, declining to provide selection judgments from individual sessions), and where confidentiality ends, then makes sure the players hear the same terms before any disclosures happen.

Players' input matters, but they can't settle a disagreement that exists between the consultant and the coach who hired them. Raising it with players first exposes them to a conflict the consultant hasn't yet resolved with the coach.

Testing for selection is a different role from confidential support, and mixing the two would make players guarded in sessions. Few sport psychology measures are designed or validated for selection decisions, so the offer adds an evidence problem to a role problem.
takeaway: When a coach or organization pays, negotiate role and information-sharing before contact with athletes, and make sure the athletes hear it too.

stem: Linnea, a conservatory pianist, self-refers for "stage nerves." In the first session, the consultant, who has had success with a structured biofeedback program, begins describing it in detail. Linnea listens quietly, then says the question really on her mind is whether she even wants a performance career. Using Bordin's model of the working alliance, what should the consultant do next?
options: Reflect her uncertainty, then offer biofeedback to ease her nerves while she decides
Set the program aside, and refer her to a career counselor for that question
Finish the program overview, then return to her career question before the session ends
Set the program aside and work out with Linnea what she wants from consulting
rationales: Reflecting her uncertainty is a good start, but offering the consultant's method while her goals are unsettled puts tasks ahead of goals. She is unlikely to commit to a task that serves a goal she hasn't chosen.

Pausing the program is right, but doubts about continuing to perform are tied to motivation and meaning, which a consultant can explore with her. Referring the question out before any goals are discussed is premature and hands off the very issue she has said matters most; a career referral may help later if specialized services are needed.

Coming back to her question is better than ignoring it, but finishing the overview first signals that the consultant's agenda comes first. In Bordin's terms, goals need to be agreed before tasks are presented.

In Bordin's model, the alliance rests on agreement on goals, agreement on the tasks that serve them, and an emotional bond. Linnea has just shown that her goals are unsettled, so the consultant pauses the method and explores and negotiates goals with her before choosing any tasks.
takeaway: Agree on goals before selecting tasks; a technique the client hasn't connected to her own goal weakens the alliance.

stem: A consultant with no para-sport experience accepts a contract with a national wheelchair rugby squad. Athletes compete under a classification system based on functional impairment, and several have recently been reclassified, which affects which lineups the coach can field. Before the first team meeting, what is the best way for the consultant to prepare?
options: Learn how classification works, and plan to ask athletes what they want understood
Ask the coach to brief the consultant on each athlete's impairment and classification
Read up on classification rules, then prepare a session on coping with reclassification
Prepare the standard workshop, and adapt it as athletes raise sport-specific issues
rationales: Competent, culturally humble practice means learning the sport's context, including how classification shapes selection, lineups, and athletes' experiences, while treating athletes as the experts on their own lives and needs rather than assuming impairment is the focus.

Gathering each athlete's impairment details from the coach makes impairment the starting point and passes along personal information the athletes haven't chosen to share. Learning the system in general is appropriate; personal details are the athletes' to share.

Learning the rules is right, but deciding before meeting the athletes that reclassification is the squad's main issue replaces assessment with assumption. The athletes' own priorities should shape the content.

Core mental skills do transfer, but waiting for athletes to raise sport-specific issues puts the burden of educating the consultant on them. Some preparation about the sport's demands is part of competence before the first meeting.
takeaway: In para sport, learn the context (including classification) and let athletes tell you what matters; impairment is not automatically the topic.

stem: Ximena, an 11-year-old gymnast, comes to a first session with her mother, who arranged it after Ximena cried at a meet. Ximena sits half behind her mother and avoids eye contact. The mother has already signed the consent forms. What should the consultant do to begin establishing a relationship with Ximena?
options: Start with a fun warm-up game, and explain what the consultant does at the next session
Ask the mother to step out so Ximena can speak more freely from the very start
Explain in simple words what the consultant does, and ask whether she would like to try
Invite Ximena to draw her favorite skill while her mother describes what happened
rationales: A game can help a shy child warm up, but postponing any explanation means Ximena takes part without knowing who the consultant is or agreeing to the work. Her assent is sought at the start, in words she understands.

Meeting alone may come later, but separating a child who is hiding behind her parent before any rapport exists is likely to raise her anxiety. Her mother's presence can be a source of safety at first.

With children, the relationship starts with a developmentally appropriate explanation of who the consultant is and what they will do together (often framed as learning skills, not fixing something wrong) and an invitation for the child's questions and agreement. This seeks her assent alongside the parent's permission.

Drawing is a child-friendly activity, but pairing it with her mother's account of the meet means Ximena is being talked about rather than talked with, and she still hasn't been told what consulting is.
takeaway: With young clients, explain the work in their language and seek their assent; parental consent alone does not build the relationship.

stem: A consultant begins the season with a collegiate men's ice hockey team whose players have never worked with a mental performance consultant. Several veterans joke that "the head doctor" is only for guys with problems. The coach has given the consultant open access to practices and travel. Which early approach is most likely to build trust with the players?
options: Ask the coach to introduce the consultant as a performance resource rather than a doctor
Attend practices and trips, learn the team's culture, and be easy to talk to informally
Open with an optional workshop showing how widely elite players use mental skills
Schedule a brief one-on-one with each player, and explain what the consultant offers
rationales: A coach's endorsement can help, but the players already see the consultant as something the coach brought in; a better introduction from the coach doesn't let them judge the consultant for themselves. Trust is built through direct contact.

Consultants whom athletes rate as effective tend to be seen as trustworthy, approachable, and able to fit in with the team's culture. Being visible at practices and on trips, learning how the team operates, and making casual contact easy lets players form their own impressions and reduces stigma.

Making the workshop optional is better than requiring it, but information about elite performers rarely shifts stigma on its own, and a presentation before any relationship exists can confirm the "head doctor" image.

Individual meetings arranged for every player feel like a requirement to skeptical veterans and put each of them in the spotlight their jokes are deflecting. Informal contact lets players engage on their own terms first.
takeaway: Early trust comes from being present, learning the culture, and being approachable, not from mandates or persuasion.

topic: Honest response to a faith question
stem: During an intake, Bilal, a professional boxer, mentions that his next fight falls during Ramadan and asks, "Have you worked with athletes who fast before?" He watches the consultant closely, as if checking whether his faith will be taken seriously. The consultant has not, and knows little about how athletes manage training while fasting. What is the best response to his question?
options: Say that they haven't, and plan to read up on fasting and training before the next session
Say that they haven't, and suggest exploring fueling around the fast with a sports dietitian
Describe how the consultant has adapted mental skills work to other athletes' schedules
Say that they haven't, and ask what fasting means for his preparation
rationales: Honesty plus self-education is part of competence, but researching it alone casts the consultant as the expert-to-be and misses the chance to learn from Bilal, who is signaling right now that he wants his practice taken seriously.

A sports dietitian may be a useful referral for fueling, but jumping to nutrition treats his question as a logistics problem and moves away from what fasting means to him. It can follow once the consultant understands his experience.
Pointing to other athletes' scheduling demands sidesteps an honest answer and implies that fasting is just another scheduling issue, which is likely to feel dismissive of his faith.

Cultural humility involves honesty about one's limits, openness, and treating the client as the expert on his own experience. An honest answer plus genuine curiosity about what fasting means for his preparation builds trust; the consultant can add consultation, reading, or a dietitian referral afterward to fill gaps.
takeaway: When you lack experience with a client's identity or practice, say so honestly and invite them to teach you what matters.

stem: A ballet company has just hired a consultant, who is introduced to the dancers at a season-opening reception. Within minutes, Aroha, a soloist, pulls the consultant aside by the buffet, describes how her mind races before solos, and asks, "So what should I do about it?" Colleagues and the artistic director are within earshot, and Aroha has not met with the consultant before. What is the best response?
options: Show interest, hold off on details, and offer a private meeting to explain the work
Offer one quick breathing tip now, and suggest she book a session if it seems to help
Move with her to a quieter corner of the room so she can keep talking more freely
Tell the artistic director she is interested, so that an intake can be arranged quickly
rationales: Informal first contacts are common in embedded roles, but the work, its confidentiality, and its limits haven't been explained yet, and she is disclosing within earshot of colleagues and her director. Responding warmly while saving details for a private first meeting, where informed consent can be covered, protects her privacy and starts the relationship on clear terms.

A tip may feel helpful, but it delivers an intervention before any assessment or consent, in a public setting, and frames the work as quick fixes. It also invites more disclosure in front of her colleagues.

A quieter corner is kinder than the buffet line, but it still turns a social event into an unstructured session before she knows how confidentiality works, and leaving together is visible to colleagues and the director.
Passing her interest to the artistic director discloses that she is seeking help to the person with the most say over her casting. She can arrange contact herself.
takeaway: When someone starts disclosing in an informal setting, respond warmly and move the conversation to a private first meeting where consent and confidentiality come first.

stem: A technology company's HR director engages a consultant to work with Soraya, a newly promoted vice president, on presenting under pressure. HR will pay and wants "to be kept in the loop." When scheduling, Soraya asked who would see her session notes. The consultant wants HR and Soraya to leave with the same understanding of goals and reporting before sessions begin. Which step best achieves this?
options: Agree on reporting with HR first, then present those terms to Soraya at her intake
Meet with Soraya first to learn her goals, then agree with HR on what it will receive
Send HR and Soraya the standard confidentiality policy and ask each to sign it
Hold one meeting with Soraya and HR to agree on goals, reporting, and what stays private
rationales: Settling terms with the sponsor first leaves Soraya to accept an arrangement she had no part in shaping, which is exactly what her question about notes suggests she is worried about.

Learning Soraya's goals first respects her, but separate conversations can leave HR and Soraya with different ideas of what "in the loop" means. A single conversation lets both hear and agree to the same terms.
A standard policy covers confidentiality in general but not the goals of this engagement or HR's specific expectations. Signing a form is not the same as negotiating a shared agreement.

In organizational work, a contracting conversation among consultant, client, and sponsor clarifies who the client is, the goals, what the sponsor will receive (such as attendance and broad progress), and what remains confidential. Holding it jointly ensures both parties hear and agree to the same terms, which is informed consent for a third-party arrangement.
takeaway: In sponsored engagements, contract with both client and sponsor at the start about goals, reporting, and confidentiality.

stem: Bordin's pantheoretical model is widely used to describe the consultant–client relationship in applied sport psychology. Which set of components makes up the working alliance in this model?
options: Empathy, congruence, and unconditional positive regard
Agreement on goals, agreement on tasks, and a bond
Closeness, commitment, complementarity, and co-orientation
Autonomy, competence, and relatedness
rationales: These are Rogers's core conditions for client-centered helping. They support the bond, but they are not Bordin's three alliance components.

Bordin described the working alliance as agreement between helper and client on the goals of the work, agreement on the tasks used to reach them, and an emotional bond of trust and attachment. The model applies across theoretical approaches.
These are Jowett's 3+1Cs of the coach–athlete relationship. They describe that dyad, not Bordin's working alliance.
These are the basic psychological needs in self-determination theory. They describe motivation, not the structure of the helping relationship.
takeaway: Bordin's working alliance = agreement on goals + agreement on tasks + an emotional bond.

stem: Ravi, a collegiate esports player, starts video sessions with a consultant. During the first session his answers grow shorter, and afterward he mentions that the consultant "seemed kind of distracted." Reviewing the recording, the consultant sees that their gaze was often directed off-screen at notes and that they showed almost no visible response while Ravi spoke. Which adjustment best improves attending in this format?
options: Explain at the start that notes are taken off-screen, then continue as before
Switch to a larger monitor and speaker view so Ravi's expressions are easier to read
Look toward the camera, keep notes brief, and show nods and encouragers on screen
Use more paraphrases and summaries so Ravi hears that he is being followed closely
rationales: Transparency about note-taking is courteous, but it leaves the behavior that read as distraction unchanged. Ravi would still be talking to someone who looks away and shows little response.

A larger view helps the consultant read Ravi, but the problem is what Ravi sees: the consultant's attending isn't visible to him. Better equipment doesn't change the consultant's gaze or responsiveness.

Ivey's attending behaviors (culturally appropriate eye contact, attentive body language, vocal qualities, and verbal tracking) need deliberate adaptation on video: looking toward the camera reads as eye contact, nods and brief encouragers must be visible on screen, and minimizing note-taking reduces the impression of distraction.

Verbal tracking is part of attending, so more paraphrasing could help, but it doesn't address the off-screen gaze and lack of visible response that Ravi noticed. The nonverbal side of attending needs fixing too.
takeaway: On video, attending must be made visible: camera-directed gaze, on-screen nods, verbal encouragers, minimal distraction.

stem: A consultant is employed by a university athletic department. In a first meeting, Aaliyah, a softball player, asks, "Do you report to Coach? Because if you do, I'm not telling you anything." Under department policy, the consultant confirms attendance to coaches only for athletes the coaches referred, and session content stays private except for safety concerns. What is the best response?
options: Explain what coaches do and don't receive, and when safety would override privacy
Ask what she is worried Coach might hear, then address that particular concern
Tell her coaches learn only about attendance, and only for athletes they refer
Give her the department's confidentiality policy and invite her to read it first
rationales: Trust grows from specific, honest information about confidentiality and its limits. Telling Aaliyah exactly what coaches would and would not learn, and when safety would override confidentiality, answers her direct question, lets her make an informed choice, and shows the consultant can be relied on.
Exploring her worry can be useful, but she has asked a direct factual question. Answering with a question can feel evasive, and addressing only her specific fear may leave other limits unexplained.

This is accurate as far as it goes, but it leaves out the safety exceptions, so it works as an implicit promise that content never leaves the room. Learning about the exceptions later would damage trust.

A written policy is a useful supplement, but handing it over instead of answering puts the work of interpretation on her and misses the chance to show, in person, that the consultant will be straight with her.
takeaway: Answer "Who do you report to?" with specific, honest limits of confidentiality; never overpromise.

topic: Communication access for a Deaf client
stem: Emeka, an elite swimmer who is Deaf, emails a consultant to begin work on race-day focus. The consultant does not use sign language and has never worked with a Deaf client. What should the consultant do to set up the first session?
options: Book a certified sign language interpreter for the first session before replying
Propose meeting by text-based chat, since Emeka chose to make contact by email
Ask his coach which communication approach works best for him at practice
Ask Emeka how he prefers to communicate, then arrange that access for the session
rationales: Arranging an interpreter is often appropriate, but booking one without asking assumes Emeka uses sign language, and which one. Preferences among Deaf clients vary (interpreting, captioning, text, or a mix).
Text chat may suit him, but inferring his preference from one email assumes rather than asks. Text-only sessions can also slow and flatten a conversation for someone who would prefer an interpreter.

The coach may know what works at the pool, but asking the coach instead of Emeka goes around the client and discloses his inquiry before he has agreed to that. He is the authority on his own communication.

Inclusive practice starts by asking the client what works for him (for example, a qualified sign language interpreter, captioning, or text) and arranging it, then speaking directly to the client rather than to any interpreter.
takeaway: Ask the client how they prefer to communicate and arrange appropriate access rather than assuming.

stem: A consultant will travel with a collegiate women's volleyball team for the first time and will stay in the team hotel at away tournaments. The coach wants the consultant available in person on trips, and several athletes have asked whether they can "just come find" the consultant. Before the first trip, what is the best step for setting expectations?
options: Ask the athletes to request travel sessions through the head coach, who will schedule them
Agree with coaches and athletes in advance on meeting times, places, and contact
Use the consultant's hotel room for sessions, keeping the door open and the times posted
Offer phone or video sessions on trips, and meet in person once the team is back on campus
rationales: Structure is good, but routing requests through the head coach tells the coach who is seeking help and may deter athletes from asking. Access to the consultant shouldn't depend on the coach knowing.

Informal settings like travel make boundary drift more likely, so expectations are set in advance: for example, availability windows, meeting in a designated room or common area, and how to make contact. Agreeing on this with coaches and athletes keeps in-person support accessible while keeping it professional.
Posted times and an open door add some structure, but a hotel room remains a private, personal space that blurs professional boundaries and creates risk for both athletes and the consultant.

Remote sessions avoid hotel-room problems, but the coach wants the consultant available in person, and tournaments are often when athletes most need face-to-face support. Clear in-person structure manages the risk without withdrawing access.
takeaway: Set travel boundaries in advance (when, where, how to reach you) so support stays available and professional.

stem: A consultant works with a collegiate water polo team under an agreement that individual sessions are confidential and that the consultant plays no part in selection or playing time. Zofia, a junior, is frustrated with her minutes and asks, "Could you mention to Coach that I want more playing time? He listens to you." She has not raised it with the coach herself. What should the consultant do?
options: Mention it to the coach in general terms, since Zofia has given her consent to share it
Offer to set up a meeting with Zofia and the coach, and help facilitate the conversation
Decline to pass it on, explain why, and help her plan how to raise it herself
Explore her frustration about minutes, and come back to the request at a later session
rationales: Consent removes the confidentiality problem but not the role problem: lobbying for minutes would make the consultant an advocate in selection, which the agreement rules out, and would change how the coach and other players see the consultant.

A facilitated meeting can sometimes help, but Zofia hasn't yet tried speaking to the coach, and mediating a playing-time dispute pulls the consultant into the selection issues the role excludes. It is premature and outside the agreed role.

Clarifying roles includes holding them when a client asks the consultant to step outside them. Declining to act as go-between, explaining that the consultant stays out of playing-time decisions, and helping Zofia plan how to raise it herself keeps the role intact and builds her own self-advocacy.

Exploring her frustration is worthwhile, but leaving the request unanswered keeps her hoping the consultant will act and postpones the role clarification. A clear, kind answer now prevents misunderstanding.
takeaway: When a client asks you to carry a message to the coach, hold your role: decline the go-between job and help the client speak for themselves.

stem: Tendai, a high school basketball player, tells the consultant, "Every time I go to the free-throw line in the fourth quarter, I already know I'm going to miss. Then Coach pulls me, and I just sit there feeling like I let everybody down." Which consultant response is the clearest reflection of feeling?
options: So late in games you expect to miss, and then Coach ends up taking you out of the game.
It sounds like you feel beaten before you shoot, and then like you've let people down.
How do you feel when you walk up to the line in the fourth quarter?
It sounds like you feel angry with Coach for pulling you late in close games.
rationales: This restates the events (content) rather than the emotions, so it is a paraphrase, not a reflection of feeling.

A reflection of feeling names the client's emotions, explicit or implied, and checks them back tentatively ("it sounds like"). Naming both the sense of defeat before the shot and the feeling of having let others down shows Tendai he has been understood at an emotional level.
This is an open question about feelings, useful for exploration, but it asks him to name emotions he has already expressed instead of reflecting them back.

This has the form of a reflection, but it names an emotion Tendai didn't express. He described defeat and letting others down, not anger at the coach, so the reflection is inaccurate and may leave him feeling misunderstood.
takeaway: A reflection of feeling accurately names the emotion beneath the words; a paraphrase restates content, and a mislabeled feeling misses the client.

stem: In their fifth session, a consultant strongly encourages Aiko, a professional ballet dancer, to adopt a new pre-performance routine. Aiko agrees. At the next session she arrives late, gives brief answers, and says the routine "was fine," in sharp contrast to her earlier openness. What should the consultant do?
options: Ask Aiko to rate how useful the routine was, then adjust it based on her rating
Offer her a choice of two alternative routines to try before her next performance
Explore what has been happening in rehearsals this week that might explain the change
Note the shift between them and ask how the last session felt to her
rationales: Seeking feedback is good practice, but rating the routine keeps the focus on the task and misses the relational signals: lateness, brief answers, and flat agreement after the consultant pushed.
Offering choices respects autonomy, but it assumes the routine is the problem and skips finding out what happened. It treats a likely strain in the relationship as a technique issue.

Outside stressors can matter, but looking only to rehearsals locates the change outside the relationship, even though it followed the consultant's push. The consultant's own part is the first thing to check.

Lateness, brief answers, and flat agreement after a push suggest a withdrawal rupture in the alliance. Repair involves immediacy: nondefensively naming the shift in the relationship, inviting her honest feedback, and accepting the consultant's own part, which often strengthens the alliance.
takeaway: Signs of withdrawal after a push suggest a rupture; repair it by using immediacy and inviting feedback nondefensively.

topic: Protecting psychological safety in a debrief
stem: During a film debrief with a collegiate women's lacrosse team, a sophomore admits she froze on a defensive assignment that led to a goal. A senior laughs and mutters, "Shocking," loudly enough for the whole room to hear. Two other players look at the floor. At the start of the season, the team agreed that mistakes would be discussed without ridicule. What should the consultant do in the moment?
options: Briefly restate the team's agreement, and thank the sophomore for owning the play
Thank the sophomore for her candor, and move on to the next clip without comment
Finish the clip, then remind the whole team of the agreement at the end of the debrief
Let the moment pass, and speak with the senior privately once the debrief is over
rationales: Psychological safety depends on the group seeing that interpersonal risk-taking, like admitting a mistake, is protected. Calmly restating the shared norm in the moment and appreciating the disclosure signals to everyone that candor is valued and ridicule is not, without shaming anyone. A private follow-up with the senior can be added later.
Thanking her reinforces candor, but leaving the comment unaddressed teaches the room that ridicule goes unchallenged, and the teammates looking at the floor will be less likely to speak up next time.

Restating the norm is right, but delaying it to the end separates the reminder from the behavior, so it reads as a general announcement rather than a response. The moment the group needed to see protected has passed.
A private conversation may also be useful, but the comment was public. Addressing it only in private leaves the group's lesson, that mockery is tolerated, in place.
takeaway: When a team norm is broken in the room, restate it briefly in the moment and reinforce the behavior you want; that is how psychological safety is maintained.

stem: Three weeks ago, Dariusz, a professional esports player, set a goal of being asleep by 1 a.m. to sharpen his reaction times. Today he says he is "fully committed" to it, then mentions he has been playing ranked matches until 4 a.m. most nights. Which response best challenges this discrepancy in a supportive way?
options: What would it take to be in bed by 1 a.m. on nights when you have ranked matches?
Why do you think the late matches keep winning out over the goal you set?
You say you're fully committed, and you've been playing until 4. How do those fit?
It sounds like you're committed, and the late nights are just hard to give up right now.
rationales: This solution-focused question is collaborative, but it jumps to planning before Dariusz has looked at the gap between his words and his behavior, so the discrepancy is never examined.
Asking "why" about a client's behavior often sounds accusatory, even when softened, and tends to invite excuses rather than reflection.

Ivey's confrontation is a supportive challenge: the consultant lays the two incongruent statements side by side without judgment and invites the client to examine them. This helps Dariusz notice the gap himself, which is more likely to prompt change.
This reflection accepts his claim of commitment at face value and smooths over the gap. It is empathic, but it doesn't challenge the discrepancy.
takeaway: Supportive confrontation names both sides of a discrepancy neutrally ("On one hand… and on the other…") and invites the client to make sense of it.

stem: Twenty minutes into a session, while recounting a recent bout, a consultant refers to Sam, a nonbinary collegiate fencer who uses they/them pronouns, as "she." Sam pauses briefly, and the consultant realizes the mistake. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Briefly apologize, restate the sentence using "they," and continue the conversation
Correct to "they" and keep going, without drawing attention to it with an apology
Apologize, and ask Sam whether there is anything the consultant should do differently
Finish the point, then apologize and correct the pronoun before the session ends
rationales: A brief acknowledgment and correction shows respect, takes responsibility, and keeps the focus on Sam's goals. The consultant then commits to getting it right, practicing outside sessions if needed.

Correcting the pronoun is essential, but skipping any acknowledgment of a slip both people noticed can come across as if it didn't register or didn't matter. A short apology takes responsibility without making it a big moment.
Asking for feedback sounds respectful, but it turns a simple correction into a conversation in which Sam has to manage the consultant's mistake and reassure them.
Delaying the correction leaves the misgendering standing for the rest of the conversation and makes the later apology a bigger, more awkward moment than an immediate fix.
takeaway: When you misgender someone, correct yourself briefly, apologize simply, and move on; don't make them comfort you.

stem: Brynja, an elite cross-country skier, has been struggling with fear of repeating a poor championship result. After saying she feels like "the only one who falls apart," she asks the consultant, a former collegiate skier, "Did you ever completely fall apart in a big race?" The consultant did, twice. Which response reflects appropriate self-disclosure?
options: Ask what prompted the question before deciding whether to share anything personal
Say yes, and describe in some detail what the consultant learned from both races
Say that many elite skiers have, and give examples from athletes the consultant knows
Briefly say yes and how it felt, then bring the focus back to Brynja
rationales: Exploring a client's question can be useful, but she has just explained why she is asking: she feels alone with this. Withholding an answer here can feel evasive and misses a chance to normalize her experience.
Sharing the consultant's lessons in detail shifts the session toward the consultant's story and turns the disclosure into advice before Brynja's own experience has been explored.
Normalizing is useful, but answering with other athletes' stories dodges her sincere question and risks sharing other people's experiences without their permission.

Self-disclosure is most helpful when it is brief, relevant, genuine, timed for the client's benefit, and followed by a return to the client. A short answer can normalize her fear and strengthen the bond without taking over the session.
takeaway: Useful self-disclosure is brief, relevant, for the client's benefit, and quickly returns the focus to the client.

stem: After a tough loss, a consultant asks Jun, a 14-year-old tennis player, "Were you nervous?" ("Kinda.") "Did you stick to your routine?" ("No.") "Do you want to work on that?" ("Sure.") The conversation stalls. Which question would best help Jun open up about the match?
options: How nervous were you between points, on a scale from 1 to 10?
What was going through your mind between points in the second set?
Why do you think you didn't use the routine you practiced all week?
What do you think we should work on before your next tournament?
rationales: A scaling question yields a useful number, but it invites a one-word answer and keeps the conversation stalled. It works better once he has started talking.

Open questions, especially those beginning with "what" or "how," invite the client to elaborate in his own words. Anchoring the question in a specific moment of the match makes it easier for a teenager to answer concretely.
Although open-ended in form, "why" questions about a lapse often sound critical and lead to defensiveness or "I don't know."

This is open-ended, but it jumps to planning before Jun has said anything about the match, and abstract future questions are hard for a shut-down teenager to answer. Exploring the experience comes first.
takeaway: When answers are one word, ask an open "what" or "how" question tied to a specific moment; avoid "why" questions about lapses and premature planning questions.

stem: Near the end of a video session, a consultant says to Captain Otieno, an Army helicopter pilot: "Okay. Your sleep has been ragged since the rotation started, the new crew member is getting under your skin, and the check ride is coming up fast. It sounds like the check ride is weighing on you most. Is that right?" Which microskill is the consultant primarily using, and for what purpose?
options: Paraphrasing, to restate the client's main point in fresh words
Reflection of feeling, to name the emotion beneath the client's words
Summarizing, to draw several themes into one statement and check accuracy
Interpretation, to offer the client a new frame for his concerns
rationales: A paraphrase restates one statement or idea. This response pulls together several themes from across the session.

The response does touch on feeling ("weighing on you"), but most of it pulls together sleep, the crew member, and the check ride, and it ends by checking accuracy. Reflecting feeling is part of it, not its main function.

Summarizing draws together multiple themes from a session, often notes how they connect or which stands out, and checks accuracy with the client. It is especially useful at transitions and before agreeing on next steps.
Interpretation offers a new perspective or meaning the client hasn't stated. Here the consultant organizes what the pilot already said rather than reframing it.
takeaway: Summaries integrate several threads and check accuracy; paraphrases restate one idea.

stem: A consultant whose own elite gymnastics career ended after years of competing through a back injury is working with Brielle, a 19-year-old collegiate gymnast who has recurring back pain. The consultant feels unusually anxious after their sessions and has twice urged Brielle to "stand up to" her coaches about training load, though Brielle has not asked for help with that. What should the consultant do about these reactions?
options: Treat the reactions as possible countertransference and take them to supervision
Ask Brielle whether she would like help talking with her coaches about training load
Refer Brielle to sports medicine for her back, and keep sessions on her own goals
Tell Brielle about the consultant's own injury history so the concern makes sense to her
rationales: The consultant's strong anxiety and push toward an agenda Brielle never set suggest the consultant's own history is shaping the work. Naming this as likely countertransference and taking it to supervision or peer consultation helps separate personal reactions from the client's goals; her pain concerns can be routed to sports medicine in the usual way.
Asking rather than urging is gentler, but the training-load agenda is still the consultant's, not Brielle's. Offering help with it keeps acting on the reaction instead of examining it.

Routing back pain to sports medicine and refocusing on her goals are both sound, but neither addresses the consultant's own reactions, which are likely to keep leaking into the work unless they are examined.
Disclosing the history to explain the concern serves the consultant's needs and adds pressure on Brielle; it is not disclosure for the client's benefit.
takeaway: Strong personal reactions and pushing your own agenda signal countertransference; take it to supervision rather than acting on it.

stem: Lior, a collegiate diver, agreed with the consultant on a goal of recovering faster after a missed dive and says the sessions feel supportive. However, Lior has skipped the agreed post-meet journaling for three weeks, explaining, "Writing stuff down just isn't me." Viewed through Bordin's working alliance, what should the consultant do?
options: Explore together what makes writing hard, and set a smaller journaling target
Revisit with Lior whether faster recovery is still the right goal for the work
Spend more session time strengthening the bond, since follow-through reflects trust
Work with Lior on a different task, such as a voice memo, that serves the same goal
rationales: Problem-solving barriers together is collaborative, but it keeps a task Lior has said doesn't fit. Shrinking the task doesn't create agreement on it.
Lior has endorsed the goal and says the sessions feel supportive. The strain is specific to the task, so reopening the goal misreads the problem.
The bond is already strong by Lior's account. Treating missed journaling as a trust problem misdiagnoses which alliance component is strained.

Bordin's model separates agreement on goals, agreement on tasks, and the bond. Here goals and bond are intact but the task isn't agreed, so the fix is to co-design a different task that serves the same goal and suits Lior.
takeaway: Diagnose which alliance component is strained; when only the task is the problem, renegotiate the task, not the goal.

topic: Adapting imagery for a wheelchair racer
stem: A consultant is introducing imagery to Kalani, an elite wheelchair racer preparing for a 1500-meter final. The consultant's standard script describes "feeling your legs drive and your feet strike the track." What is the best way to adapt the imagery for Kalani?
options: Rewrite the script around arm and push sensations, and have Kalani try it this week
Build the script with Kalani around her own stroke, chair, and race sensations
Keep the standard script but use an external visual view so legs aren't mentioned
Ask the coach to describe the race sensations so the script is technically accurate
rationales: Adapting to upper-body movement is the right direction, but writing it alone relies on the consultant's guesses about how Kalani races. Her own sensations (trunk position, gloves, chair contact) are best captured with her.

PETTLEP-based imagery stresses matching the physical, task, and environmental details of the athlete's real performance. Co-creating the script with Kalani around her pushing stroke, chair, and race sensations makes it more effective and respects her as the expert on her own sport.
Switching to an external visual perspective sidesteps the mismatch but drops kinesthetic detail, a strength of good imagery, and the script still isn't built from her actual race.
The coach may offer useful technical input, but going to the coach rather than Kalani sidelines the athlete, who knows best what racing feels like from the chair.
takeaway: Individualize imagery to the athlete's real movements and equipment, built with the athlete.

topic: Client friend request on social media
stem: After a strong season of work together, Alejandro, a 24-year-old professional cyclist, sends a follow request to the consultant's personal Instagram account with a message: "Let's keep in touch here—way easier than email!" They are still actively working together. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Accept, and move him to a restricted list that hides the consultant's personal posts
Accept, and agree together to keep session topics off the platform
Decline warmly, explain why, and keep contact on the professional channels
Decline without comment, and explain the boundary only if Alejandro raises it
rationales: A restricted list limits what he sees but still creates a personal connection with a current client, a multiple relationship that can blur roles and expose both people's information.

Agreeing on ground rules is collaborative, but it accepts the personal connection the boundary is meant to prevent. The concern isn't only what gets discussed online; it's the dual relationship itself.

Managing multiple relationships, including on social media, is part of professional responsibility. Warmly declining, explaining why (ideally covered in a social media policy at intake), and offering the professional channels keeps the boundary clear while preserving the relationship.
Declining is right, but leaving the reason unexplained may confuse or hurt Alejandro and could be read as rejection. Boundaries work best when they are explained, not left to be discovered.
takeaway: Don't connect with current clients on personal social media; explain why kindly and keep contact professional.

stem: At 11 p.m. during an away tournament, Destiny, a 20-year-old collegiate field hockey player, knocks on the consultant's hotel room door. She is upset after being benched, says she won't be able to sleep until she talks to someone, and asks to come in. She is not in danger. What should the consultant do?
options: Talk with her briefly in a quiet corner of the lobby, then plan a fuller session tomorrow
Invite her in briefly with the door propped open, since she is an adult athlete
Ask her to return to her room, and offer a full session first thing in the morning
Suggest she call the after-hours counseling line tonight, then meet with her tomorrow
rationales: Moving to a common space keeps support available tonight while maintaining a professional boundary. A short, contained conversation in a quiet, semi-public spot protects both her privacy and the integrity of the relationship, and a fuller session can follow in a proper setting.
An open door doesn't change that a consultant's hotel room late at night is a private, personal space. It invites boundary blurring and misperception regardless of the athlete's age.
A morning session holds the boundary, but sending away a distressed adult athlete who can't sleep, when support can be offered appropriately now, is unnecessarily rejecting and may damage trust.

A crisis or counseling line fits risk or a mental health emergency; she is upset about being benched and is not in danger. Redirecting her there treats ordinary distress as a crisis and leaves her without the support she asked for.
takeaway: On the road, meet athletes in appropriate common spaces rather than hotel rooms, even when the request is sincere and the need is real.

stem: A consultant receives a referral for Riley, a transgender woman on a university swim team, who wants help managing pre-race anxiety. The consultant has extensive experience with competitive anxiety but no training in working with transgender clients and worries about saying the wrong thing. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Refer Riley to a consultant who specializes in working with transgender athletes
Begin the anxiety work while seeking training and consultation on affirming practice
Complete training in affirming practice first, and start sessions in about a month
Accept, and ask her to educate the consultant about transgender athletes in general
rationales: Riley's request is pre-race anxiety, which is within the consultant's competence. Referring because of her identity is unnecessary and can feel rejecting; competence is judged against the presenting concern, with cultural knowledge built alongside.

The competence standard asks consultants to practice within their training and to take reasonable steps (education, consultation, supervision) to serve diverse clients well. The presenting concern is squarely within the consultant's competence, so the consultant proceeds while developing cultural competence in affirming practice and following Riley's lead on what is relevant.
Building knowledge is right, but delaying a request the consultant is already competent to handle leaves Riley without support for a month. Training and consultation can happen alongside the work.

Following a client's lead about her own experience is good practice, but asking her to educate the consultant about transgender athletes in general shifts the consultant's learning burden onto the client.
takeaway: A client's identity is not a reason to refer; work within your competence on the presenting concern and build cultural competence alongside.

topic: Conflict of interest in a small community
stem: A consultant in a small town is approached by the parents of Ethan, a 16-year-old club baseball pitcher. The consultant's own son pitches for the same team, the two boys compete for starts, and the families share carpools to games. Another qualified consultant in the next town offers in-person and virtual sessions. The parents say they chose this consultant because "you already know everybody." What should the consultant do?
options: Accept, after disclosing the son's role to the parents in a signed consent form
Accept, with a colleague supervising the case to monitor the consultant's objectivity
Ask Ethan whether he is comfortable working with a teammate's parent before deciding
Explain the conflict to the parents and refer them to the other consultant
rationales: Informed consent about a conflict is necessary but not sufficient. Disclosure doesn't remove the consultant's stake in which boy gets starts, or the difficulty Ethan would have speaking openly about a rival who is his consultant's son.

Supervision can help manage an unavoidable overlap, but it can't remove a direct conflict of interest involving the consultant's own child, especially when a qualified alternative is readily available.

Ethan's comfort matters, but a 16-year-old may not feel free to object, and his comfort doesn't address the consultant's impaired objectivity. The consultant is responsible for resolving the conflict, not the client.

Multiple relationships aren't automatically unethical, but they should be avoided when they could reasonably be expected to impair objectivity or harm the client. With the consultant's son competing directly with Ethan and an accessible alternative nearby, transparently explaining the conflict and referring is the most protective choice.
takeaway: When an overlapping relationship creates a real conflict of interest and a qualified alternative exists, explain the conflict and refer.

stem: Over two months, Noor, a 26-year-old professional squash player, has begun texting the consultant late at night with updates, calling the consultant "the only one who really gets me," and asking for reassurance before every match. The consultant's stated policy, agreed at intake, is that texts are for scheduling only. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Reply once by text restating the policy, then answer only scheduling messages
Agree to a short reassurance text before each match, since that seems to help her
Raise the pattern in session, restate the policy, and explore what Noor needs
Refer Noor to a counselor to address her growing reliance on the consultant
rationales: Restating the policy is right, but doing it by text and then going quiet skips the conversation about what is driving the pattern. Without that, the boundary may feel like rejection, and her underlying need goes unaddressed.
Pre-match reassurance is warm, but it formalizes the dependence the pattern shows and moves contact further from the agreed policy. It also delays her developing her own pre-match routine.

Idealization and growing reliance on the consultant are common relationship dynamics (sometimes understood as transference). The practical response is to name the pattern warmly in session, restate the boundary consistently, and explore what Noor needs, such as her own pre-match routine or other supports, while staying alert to signs that a mental health referral is warranted.

Referral may become appropriate if signs of a mental health concern emerge, but nothing described so far requires it, and referring before discussing the pattern can feel like being passed along. The dynamic can first be addressed within the relationship.
takeaway: When a client leans on you beyond agreed limits, address it openly and keep the boundary consistent rather than over-responding or withdrawing.

stem: A consultant has worked for a year with Folake, a professional surfer who just won her first major event. That evening, Folake posts publicly and tags the consultant's practice account: "Couldn't have done it without my mental performance coach!" She then texts the consultant, "Repost it—you deserve the business!" They are still working together. What should the consultant do?
options: Repost it, since Folake wrote it freely and wasn't asked for it
Thank her, and ask her to remove the tag so the relationship stays confidential
Repost it with a note that individual results vary and success isn't guaranteed
Thank her warmly, and explain why the practice won't share or repost it
rationales: An unsolicited testimonial is still a testimonial. Reposting it uses a current client's endorsement to market the consultant's services, which the Ethics Code does not allow, because a current client's dependence on the relationship makes such an endorsement hard to treat as freely given.

Declining to amplify the post is appropriate, but Folake is free to share her own experience, including that she works with a consultant. Asking her to change her post polices her disclosure instead of managing the consultant's own conduct.
Disclaimers can make advertising more accurate, but they don't change that the content is a testimonial from a current client. The problem is using her endorsement at all, not how it is qualified.

The Ethics Code bars testimonials from current clients, and reposting or sharing her post would turn it into the consultant's advertising. Thanking her warmly and briefly explaining the rule respects her excitement and her right to post about her own experience while keeping the consultant from using it for promotion.
takeaway: A current client's unsolicited praise is still a testimonial; thank them, but don't repost it or use it to market your services.

topic: One-on-one with a minor while traveling
stem: At a national youth championship, Pavel, a 15-year-old wrestler on a team covered by the U.S. Center for SafeSport's Minor Athlete Abuse Prevention Policies, asks the traveling consultant to talk privately about nerves before his first match, which is about an hour away. Teammates are around the hotel, and the consultant's room is down the hall. Where should this conversation take place?
options: In the consultant's room with the door open, after texting a parent for permission
In a quiet corner of the team area, where others can see them but not overhear
In a private meeting room, with an assistant coach sitting in on the conversation
After his match, when one of his parents can join them for the conversation
rationales: A hotel room is a private space that is neither readily observable nor interruptible, and a parent's permission doesn't override MAAPP's requirements for one-on-one interactions with minor athletes. An open door doesn't change the setting.

MAAPP requires one-on-one interactions between adults and minor athletes to be observable and interruptible. A quiet spot in a common team area lets Pavel speak privately in tone while remaining in view of others, protecting both him and the consultant, and it fits the hour before his match.

A second adult makes the meeting compliant, but MAAPP doesn't require one, and adding an assistant coach to a private conversation about nerves gives up the privacy Pavel asked for when an observable, interruptible space would do.
Waiting for a parent goes beyond what the policy requires and leaves Pavel without support at the moment he asked for it, just before his match.
takeaway: Under MAAPP, one-on-one conversations with minor athletes happen in observable and interruptible spaces, not hotel rooms; a parent's permission doesn't change that.
